records.location: Tonle Sap from Chroy Changvar bridge to Kampong Chhnang province; Mekong from Koh Rokar area in Kandal province to Kampong Cham province, Cambodia
records.summary: According to the article, Minister of Mines and Energy Keo Rattanak said on 15 February, at the 2026 annual mineral products exhibition, that the Cambodian government has ordered the relevant ministries to dredge sand in the middle of the Tonle Sap from the Chroy Changvar bridge to Kampong Chhnang province, and in the Mekong from the Koh Rokar area in Kandal province to Kampong Cham province. The stated purpose is to open waterways so that large ships can carry goods in and out via the Funan Techo canal. The minister said the dredging will not cause riverbank collapse, but environmental experts worry about impacts, especially bank erosion, if impacts are not clearly studied. The cover photo shows a sand dredging barge in Koh Rokar 2 commune, Mukh Kampul district. The supplied text is only an introduction to a radio programme, with no further detail.
records.limitations: Only a short programme teaser is available. The audio content is not included, and no volumes, dredging scale, or expert names are given. Summarised from the Khmer text in English only. Automated English summary; native-language review may be needed.

records.location: Mekong Delta (ĐBSCL), Vietnam, including Tien River in Dong Thap, Vam Nao River in Cho Moi, An Giang, and Hau River
records.summary: Tuổi Trẻ reports on a workshop held 16 June organised by the Vietnam Hydraulic Association and the HCMC Hydraulic Science Association. Papers reportedly agreed on recommending an end to sand mining in the Mekong Delta; delegates said that without stopping it the delta would be in danger within a few decades. A Marine Engineering Institute report said that since 2005 erosion on the Tien River in Dong Thap has been intense; Đỗ Hoài Nam stated that 101 km of the 122.9 km main channel in Dong Thap is eroded, nearly 300 ha of bank land was lost in 2005-2016, and losses were estimated at about 320 billion dong. A 24 April landslide on the Vam Nao River in Cho Moi, An Giang, reportedly destroyed 16 houses. Scientists attributed erosion to flood flows, reduced sand from upstream Mekong structures, and excessive sand mining. Research data cited say sediment reaching the delta from upstream is only about 30 million tonnes per year, while licensed sand extraction (excluding illegal mining) is reportedly comparable. Some participants proposed a total ban, while others said only reduced extraction is feasible now because of high construction demand and no substitutes.
records.limitations: News report of workshop presentations; underlying studies are not detailed, and the sediment and mining figures are cited without methodology. Licensed mining volume is only said to be roughly equal to 30 million tonnes per year, with no separate exact figure. Automated English summary; native-language review may be needed.

The Mekong stretch (Koh Rokar area, Kandal, to Kampong Cham), the Tonle Sap stretch (Chroy Changvar bridge to Kampong Chhnang) and the Cambodia attribution are all stated in the text. The 15 February statement is attributed to Minister Keo Rattanak, and the experts' concern is attributed to environmental experts. The draft's numbers are all dates, and the 17/02/2026 publication date is quoted exactly from the body. No volumes are claimed. The draft correctly notes that the text is only a short programme teaser. The nearby archive record MSW-058 is a different event, a study on Tonle Sap reverse flow, so this is not a duplicate. One minor caveat is that the draft's 'full body' readType slightly overstates what was supplied, but the limitations field discloses this.
